passage:
Teacher's note, Class 3, Thursday. Written by Jaya Ma'am.

In today's quick-quiz I asked, "Which is heavier: one kilo of cotton or one kilo of iron?" Rohit shouted, "Iron!" and the whole row repeated it. Jasleen, eight, sat very still. I saw her whisper "same" to herself and start writing it on her slate. Then she looked around at everyone saying iron. She rubbed out "same" with her sleeve and wrote "iron". When a boy laughed at Manu for a wrong answer earlier, Jasleen had laughed too, and I think she remembered it. At break she came to my desk and asked quietly, "Ma'am, is it the same?" I said yes. She looked at her grey sleeve.

What I did next: from tomorrow, children will write answers on their slates privately before anyone speaks.

qa.q: What did Jasleen first write on her slate?
qa.a: She started writing 'same' on her slate.

qa.q: Why did Jasleen rub out her answer?
qa.a: She was worried about being laughed at for being the only one to disagree, since the whole row was saying iron and she had seen Manu laughed at.

qa.q: Why is the teacher's new rule a good step?
qa.a: Writing answers privately before anyone speaks lets children like Jasleen keep their own answer without feeling the pressure of the group.

qa.q: How might Manu feel about quiz time after being laughed at earlier?
qa.a: Manu may feel nervous and embarrassed, and less willing to answer aloud, just as the laughter made Jasleen afraid to disagree.

grounding: An eight-year-old knows the right answer but switches to the group's wrong answer because disagreeing alone feels risky.

passage:
Saturday

Scouts map day. We had to find the old well using the map and a compass. Joseph was holding the map and said, "The stream goes this way, towards the hill." Everyone said, "Yes, yes, hill." I looked at the compass. The needle said the stream was going the other way. I was nearly sure.

But Joseph is the patrol leader, and all five of them were already walking. If I said "wrong way" and I was wrong, they'd call me Compass Girl for the whole camp. So I walked behind them and didn't say anything.

We walked for twenty minutes and ended up at a cow shed. Then Joseph turned the map around and went red. We went back the way I thought.

Nobody knew I had known. I feel stupid for being right and quiet.

- Gurleen

qa.q: Where did the patrol end up after walking for twenty minutes?
qa.a: They ended up at a cow shed.

qa.q: Why did Gurleen keep quiet even though the compass showed the other way?
qa.a: She was afraid that if she spoke alone and was wrong, the others would tease her and call her Compass Girl for the whole camp.

qa.q: What could Gurleen try next time she is nearly sure the group is wrong?
qa.a: She could quietly show Joseph the compass and ask Joseph to check, which is less scary than announcing that everyone is wrong.

qa.q: How might Joseph feel on learning Gurleen had known the right way?
qa.a: Joseph might feel embarrassed but also wish she had spoken, since it would have saved the whole patrol twenty minutes.

grounding: A ten-year-old sees the compass contradict the group but follows everyone, worried about being laughed at if she disagrees alone.

passage: Arohi, come sit with your Manjula Nani. You say your friends all think that new girl is stuck-up, and now you think so too? Let me tell you something. When I was fifteen, a girl called Kamini joined our school in Pune. She wore thick glasses and wrote poems in the back of her maths notebook. I liked her. She lent me her poems once, and I thought they were beautiful. But my group decided she was proud. "She thinks she's better than us." Everyone said it, every day. At first I just kept quiet. Then, slowly, I began to see it too. Her silence looked like pride. Her poems looked like showing off. By the end of the year I really believed it. Years later I met her at a wedding. She was only shy, beta. She had always been shy. I had stopped trusting my own eyes.

qa.q: Where did Kamini write her poems?
qa.a: She wrote them in the back of her maths notebook.

qa.q: How did Manjula come to think about Kamini over the year?
qa.a: At first she only kept quiet, but slowly she started to believe the group, until Kamini's silence and poems looked like pride to her.

qa.q: What could Arohi do differently from what her Nani did?
qa.a: Arohi could spend a little time with the new girl herself and trust what she sees, instead of letting her friends' opinion replace her own.

qa.q: What might that year have been like for Kamini?
qa.a: Kamini was probably lonely and confused, being treated as proud by a whole group when she was only shy.

grounding: An elder recalls how, at fifteen, she first stayed silent and then truly came to share her group's harsh view of a classmate, doubting her own judgement.

passage: The inter-school music contest was running late, the hall was roaring, and the student judges had ten minutes to hand in their scores. Tenzin, sixteen, had given the second band, the quiet one with the flute, a nine. The loud band with the drummer got a six from him; they'd been out of time twice. Then he looked up. Sudha and the other four judges were all saying the same thing: "The drummer band killed it. Best by miles." "Honestly, the flute band was boring." Tenzin's pen hovered. Maybe he'd been sitting too near the speaker. Maybe he didn't really understand fast music. Everyone else couldn't be wrong. With the teacher calling "Two minutes!", he crossed out his six and wrote eight, then crossed the nine and wrote seven. Walking out, he wondered: had he changed his mind, or only his numbers?

qa.q: What score did Tenzin first give the flute band?
qa.a: He first gave the flute band a nine.

qa.q: What was Tenzin thinking as his pen hovered over the scores?
qa.a: He was doubting his own ears, wondering if he'd been too near the speaker or didn't understand fast music, since everyone else agreed.

qa.q: What could Tenzin have done with the little time he had?
qa.a: He could have kept his scores and written one line explaining that the drummer band was out of time twice, trusting what he actually heard.

qa.q: How might the flute band feel if they lost by a small margin?
qa.a: They might feel disappointed without knowing that at least one judge had honestly thought they were the best.

grounding: A teenager changes his judging scores to match a unanimous group, unsure whether he truly changed his mind or only stayed in line.

passage: The student council in Clara's school in Vienna was voting on a new rule: no phones at all during lunch, not even in bags. The class rep said, "Hands up if you agree," and hand after hand went up. Clara, fourteen, raised hers too, though she had a doubt. Then Hana, from the back, kept her hand down and said, "Wait. What about people who need to call home? My mum works nights, she texts me at lunch." The room went silent. Then Felix lowered his hand. "My little brother gets picked up by me. I need my phone." Two more hands dropped. Then Clara's. Within a minute, half the class was suggesting changes: phones allowed in bags, calls in the corridor. Clara watched it happen and thought how nobody had moved until Hana did.

qa.q: What rule was the student council voting on?
qa.a: A rule of no phones at all during lunch, not even in bags.

qa.q: What does Clara lowering her hand after Hana spoke suggest about her?
qa.a: It suggests she had her own doubt all along but did not dare show it until someone else spoke first.

qa.q: What choice gave the class a better rule, and why?
qa.a: Hana's decision to keep that hand down and explain the reason gave others the support they needed to share their own concerns, so the rule could be improved.

qa.q: How might Hana have felt as the first one to disagree?
qa.a: Hana was probably nervous speaking against a room full of raised hands, and relieved when Felix and others joined in.

grounding: A student watches one classmate voice doubt about a popular rule and sees others quickly dare to disagree once they have a supporter.

passage: At the coaching centre, the whole Class 12 batch was signing a complaint against Mr Iyer, the physics teacher. "Too strict, too fast," the letter said. Thirty signatures filled the page. Jagdish, seventeen, sat by the window watching the paper go round. When it reached Hansa, she didn't sign. She said, not loudly, "Has anyone actually talked to him first? He did stay back two hours for us before the mock." Silence. Then Ravi said, "Yeah... he helped me with rotation." Another student put her pen down. "Maybe we just ask him to slow down." In five minutes the letter was folded away and three students were volunteering to speak to Mr Iyer after class. Jagdish kept thinking about it on the bus. Twenty-nine people had signed without a word. It had taken only one voice to make the others remember what they really thought.

qa.q: How many signatures were already on the complaint?
qa.a: Thirty signatures filled the page.

qa.q: What was Hansa thinking when she didn't sign?
qa.a: She was doubtful that a complaint was fair, remembering that Mr Iyer had stayed back two hours for them before the mock.

qa.q: What did the batch decide to do instead, and why was it better?
qa.a: Three students chose to speak to Mr Iyer directly and ask him to slow down, which gave him a chance to respond instead of facing a group complaint.

qa.q: How might Mr Iyer have felt if the complaint had gone ahead?
qa.a: He might have felt hurt and blindsided, especially after staying back two hours to help the students.

grounding: A student observes how one classmate's doubt about a group complaint quickly frees others to disagree with the majority.

passage:
Faculty adviser's note, debating society, 16 September. Written by Vaibhav Sir.

Today's committee meeting voted on whether to disqualify a rival college's speaker for arriving five minutes late to the final. Eleven members voted yes. Yash, twenty, voted no. He said, "The rules say ten minutes, and it was the bus strike. We'd want the same if it were us."

I watched what followed. Several members stared at him; one muttered, "Whose side are you on?" The president asked him twice if he was "sure". Yash's voice stayed level, but his hands were locked together under the table, and he looked at the rulebook, then at me, as if checking he had read it right. After the meeting nobody walked out with him.

What I did next: I checked the rulebook. He was right. I told the committee the speaker stays, and I thanked Yash privately.

qa.q: How many members voted to disqualify the speaker?
qa.a: Eleven members voted yes.

qa.q: What do Yash's locked hands and his glance at the rulebook suggest?
qa.a: They suggest he was under strain and doubting himself for a moment, checking he was right even while keeping his voice level.

qa.q: Why did it matter that Vaibhav Sir checked the rulebook and thanked Yash?
qa.a: It confirmed Yash was right and showed him his courage was noticed, which matters when standing alone has cost him socially.

qa.q: How did the other committee members see Yash during the vote?
qa.a: Many saw him as disloyal, asking whose side he was on, and none walked out with him afterwards.

grounding: A young adult who alone disagrees with his committee faces stares, pressure and self-doubt, and his stance costs him socially though he is right.

passage:
Tuesday night

All forty of us were supposed to walk out of tomorrow's statistics exam, because the professor added one question from outside the syllabus. The class group had forty thumbs-up. Then it was my turn, and I wrote, "I don't want to walk out. It's one question out of ten. Can we ask for it to be dropped instead?"

The chat went silent for ten minutes. Then: "Rafiq wants marks more than friends." "Traitor." "Enjoy writing alone."

In the canteen people stopped talking when I sat down. I kept thinking, maybe I'm wrong. Maybe I'm just scared. Forty people can't all be wrong.

Disha messaged me privately: "I agree with you. But I can't say it in the group." That helped a little. Also made it lonelier.

I'm still going to write the exam. My hands are cold just thinking about walking in.

qa.q: How many thumbs-up did the walkout plan get in the class group?
qa.a: The class group had forty thumbs-up.

qa.q: How did Rafiq feel after the chat went silent and the insults came?
qa.a: Rafiq felt isolated and full of self-doubt, wondering whether this was being right or just being scared, with cold hands at the thought of the exam.

qa.q: What could Disha do that would make Rafiq's stand easier?
qa.a: Disha could say 'I agree' in the group, because one open supporter would make Rafiq far less alone and might free others to speak.

qa.q: Why might Disha agree privately but stay quiet in the group?
qa.a: Disha is likely afraid of being called a traitor too, so the support for Rafiq stays private where the others cannot see.

grounding: A young adult who alone disagrees with the class walkout faces silence, insults and self-doubt, showing the social cost and courage of dissent.

passage: The grant application was due at five, and at two o'clock the NGO team was still arguing about which district to target. Everyone favoured Rampur: it was nearest, and their director liked it. Naveen, twenty-five, wasn't sure. With the clock running, he spent ten minutes checking the census tables on his laptop and asked Usha to look over his numbers. Then he said, "I might be wrong, but Sitapur has almost twice as many girls out of school as Rampur. Can I show you?" He shared his screen. The director frowned. "Rampur has better roads." "That's fair," Naveen said. "Travel cost matters. Could we include both, with Sitapur as the main one?" Usha pointed out that Sitapur's numbers were three years old. Naveen nodded. "Good catch. Let's say that openly in the application." They submitted at 4:52, with both districts.

qa.q: Which district did Naveen's numbers point to?
qa.a: Sitapur, which had almost twice as many girls out of school as Rampur.

qa.q: What does Naveen's 'That's fair' show about his attitude?
qa.a: It shows he felt open and unthreatened by other views, caring more about the best answer than about winning the argument.

qa.q: Which of Naveen's choices helped the team reach a better decision under pressure?
qa.a: Checking the numbers, asking Usha to review them and stating his view with evidence, while accepting good objections, led to a stronger application.

qa.q: How might the director have felt when Naveen disagreed?
qa.a: The director may have been annoyed at first, but Naveen's polite tone and evidence made it easier to consider a different choice.

grounding: A young professional checks his reasoning, disagrees politely with evidence under time pressure, and stays open to correction.

passage: The architecture office in Chennai was buzzing: everyone loved the new glass front for the school building. Disha, twenty-four, did too, at first. That night she worried. The building faced west. She checked the sun paths twice and sent her sums to Leela, a senior she trusted, asking, "Am I missing something?" Leela replied, "Your numbers look right. Ask it as a question." At Friday's review, when the principal architect asked, "All agreed?", Disha said, "Can I ask one thing first? The classrooms face west. Have we checked how hot they'll get after two?" A few people looked surprised. She showed her sums calmly. The principal architect raised an objection: special glass could cut the heat. "I didn't think of that," Disha said. "Could we compare the cost?" The team agreed to test both options before deciding.

qa.q: Which direction did the building face?
qa.a: The building faced west.

qa.q: How can you tell Disha wanted to be sure before speaking up?
qa.a: She checked the sun paths twice and asked Leela if she was missing something, showing she doubted herself and wanted to test her reasoning.

qa.q: What turning point in the review led to a better choice?
qa.a: When Disha asked a question instead of attacking the design and admitted she hadn't thought of special glass, the team agreed to test both options.

qa.q: How might the children who will study in those classrooms be affected?
qa.a: If the heat is checked now, they may get cooler, more comfortable classrooms in the afternoons.

grounding: A young architect checks her reasoning, raises a different view politely as a question with evidence, and stays open to being wrong.

passage:
Playschool note, Grandparents' Day. Written by Zainab Ma'am.

Vikas, four, was thrilled when his Nana arrived. He pushed the bigger half of his laddoo into Nana's mouth, laughing. Then Pooja's cousin, visiting for the day, came and stood next to him, looking at the box. Vikas pulled the box close and turned his back. When I asked if she could have one, he whispered, "She's not my family." At last, with Nana nodding, he held out the smallest piece.

What I did next: I sat them together for the clay game, so they would not be strangers.

qa.q: Who did Vikas give the bigger half of his laddoo to?
qa.a: He gave it to his Nana.

qa.q: Why did Vikas whisper 'She's not my family'?
qa.a: He felt close and generous with his Nana but unsure and less willing to share with a child he did not know.

qa.q: How did the teacher help, and why might it work?
qa.a: She sat the two children together for the clay game so they could get to know each other, which could make sharing feel easier next time.

qa.q: How might Pooja's cousin feel when Vikas turns his back?
qa.a: The visiting child might feel left out and shy, standing near a box of sweets in a place where she knows almost no one.

grounding: A four-year-old shares eagerly with his grandfather but is slow to share with a visiting stranger's child.

passage: In the courtyard of their village house, Lakshmi, five, sat with a ripe guava. She bit it, then held it up. "Ammamma, you have!" Ammamma took a tiny bite and laughed. Lakshmi gave a big piece to her little brother too. Then the milkman came with his small son, who stood by the gate staring. Lakshmi hid the guava behind her back. Her big sister Alka said, "Share one piece?" Lakshmi shook her head. "He's not ours." Alka waited. The boy kept looking. At last Lakshmi walked over and held out a small piece, then ran back to Ammamma's lap.

qa.q: Who did Lakshmi give the first bite of her guava to?
qa.a: She gave it to Ammamma.

qa.q: What does Lakshmi hiding the guava suggest about how she feels?
qa.a: It suggests she feels generous with her own family but shy and protective with a boy she does not know.

qa.q: What did Alka do that helped Lakshmi share?
qa.a: Alka asked gently and then waited, giving Lakshmi time to decide for herself instead of forcing her.

qa.q: What is it like for the milkman's son standing at the gate?
qa.a: He is a visitor watching other children share a treat, which might make him feel shy and left out.

grounding: A five-year-old happily shares with her grandmother and brother but is slow to share with the milkman's son.

passage: That morning Deepika, ten, and her brother Varun had fought over the TV remote so loudly that Mummy took it away. "You're the worst brother ever," Deepika said, and didn't talk to him at breakfast. In the evening, at the park in their Nagpur colony, Varun was flying his new kite. A bigger boy from the next building, maybe twelve, grabbed the string and yanked it. The kite tore on a branch. "Baby kite for a baby," the boy said. Varun's chin shook. Deepika was across the park on the swings. She jumped off and ran over, her heart hammering. "Give that string back. He's my brother." The boy was taller, but she didn't move. He dropped the string and walked off. Deepika picked up the torn kite, smoothed it and handed it to Varun. She still didn't say sorry about the remote.

qa.q: What did the bigger boy do to Varun's kite?
qa.a: He grabbed the string and yanked it, and the kite tore on a branch.

qa.q: How can you tell Deepika was scared when she stood up to the boy?
qa.a: Her heart was hammering and the boy was taller, but she still did not move.

qa.q: What choice did Deepika make, and why does it matter?
qa.a: She put aside the morning's fight and ran to defend Varun, showing that family loyalty mattered more to her than the grudge.

qa.q: How might Varun see his sister after the park?
qa.a: Varun may feel protected and surprised, knowing his sister stood up for him on the same day she called him the worst brother.

grounding: A girl who fought with her brother that morning still rushes to defend him from a bigger boy, as family loyalty overrides the grudge.

passage:
"You broke my pencil box, Chinmay! I'm never lending you anything again." Charu slammed her door that morning.

In the afternoon their cousin Neeraj, fourteen, came to stay.
"What's this?" Neeraj held up Chinmay's drawing. "A dog? Looks like a potato."
Chinmay, eight, reached for it. "Give it back."
"Potato-dog! Potato-dog!" Neeraj held it over his head.
Charu came out of her room. "Neeraj bhaiya, give it back."
"Why? You're not even talking to him."
"He's still my brother." Her voice wobbled, but she held out her hand. "Give it. Now."
Neeraj rolled his eyes and handed it over. "Fine. So touchy."
Charu gave the drawing to Chinmay. "It's a good dog."
"You're not angry any more?"
"I'm still angry about the pencil box," Charu said. "That's different."

qa.q: What did Neeraj say Chinmay's drawing looked like?
qa.a: He said it looked like a potato.

qa.q: What does Charu's wobbling voice suggest when she faces Neeraj?
qa.a: It suggests she was nervous standing up to an older cousin but did it anyway to protect her brother.

qa.q: What does Charu's last line teach about family loyalty?
qa.a: It shows she can stay angry about the pencil box and still defend Chinmay, because loyalty to him matters more than the grudge.

qa.q: How might Chinmay feel about his sister after this?
qa.a: Chinmay might feel relieved and loved, surprised that the sister who slammed her door in the morning stood up for him.

grounding: A girl defends her little brother from an older cousin's teasing on the same day she quarrelled with him, showing loyalty over a grudge.

subtype: Duty to family versus own wishes [Actor]
passage:
Monday. Vijay, sixteen, found out he'd been picked for the state football trials in Pune, a week away. He ran all the way home. His father was lying down, recovering from a fall, and the family tea stall had been shut for three days. His younger brother Kunal's entrance coaching started the same week.

Wednesday. Vijay stood behind the tea stall at six in the morning, pouring chai for the bus drivers, so Kunal could go to coaching and the stall wouldn't lose customers. He told the coach he couldn't come. When Kunal left with his bag, Vijay gave him ten rupees for the bus and ruffled his hair.

Saturday. The trials were that day. Between customers Vijay kept checking the time. At noon he pictured the other boys running onto the field and slammed the kettle down too hard. That night Kunal came home and said, "Bhaiya, I got the full test right." Vijay hugged him, and meant it.

qa.q: What was Vijay picked for?
qa.a: He was picked for the state football trials in Pune.

qa.q: What did Vijay feel at noon on Saturday, and what shows it?
qa.a: He felt resentment and loss, picturing the other boys on the field and slamming the kettle down too hard.

qa.q: What choice did Vijay make, and what did it cost him?
qa.a: He chose to run the stall so Kunal could attend coaching, which helped the family but cost him the trials he had dreamed of.

qa.q: How might Kunal see his brother's sacrifice?
qa.a: Kunal may not fully know what Vijay gave up, but coming home proud of his test shows the sacrifice is helping him.

grounding: A teenage boy gives up football trials to run the family stall so his brother can study, feeling love and resentment together.

subtype: Duty to family versus own wishes [Actor]
passage: Himani, you asked me why I never went to college. Sit, I'll tell you. When I was sixteen, I got a place at the district college in Nashik for science. I still remember the letter. But that same year your great-grandfather's crops failed, and there was only money for one of us. My little brother, your Nana, was clever at maths. So I told my mother, "Send him. I'll help at home." She cried and held my face. I meant it, beta, truly. I loved that boy. I stitched blouses at night to pay for his books. But when he came home in his college shirt, I went behind the cowshed and cried, angry at no one. I kept the college letter in my trunk for forty years. I am proud of him. I also wish I'd gone. Both, Himani. Your Urmila Dadi feels both.

qa.q: Where did Urmila get a place to study science?
qa.a: She got a place at the district college in Nashik.

qa.q: What was Urmila feeling when her brother came home in his college shirt?
qa.a: She felt a painful mix of love and resentment, which made her go behind the cowshed and cry, angry at no one.

qa.q: What turning point shaped the rest of Urmila's life, and what does she say about it now?
qa.a: Choosing to send her brother instead of herself when money ran short; she says she is proud of him and also wishes she had gone.

qa.q: How might Himani feel hearing her Dadi's story?
qa.a: Himani might feel moved and understand that Himani's Dadi's sacrifice for the family was real, and also that it cost her something big.

grounding: An elder recalls giving up college at sixteen so her brother could study, feeling love and resentment together, both lasting for years.

passage: "Zainab, it's me, Aditi, the girl who can't keep quiet. Can I tell you something weird about my coaching centre job? I just file papers there part-time. Last week they needed a new maths teacher for the evening batch. Two people gave demo classes. One was a woman who'd taught for five years; the kids actually clapped at the end of her demo. The other was Rohit, the owner's nephew, who mumbled and got a sum wrong. The owner gave it to Rohit. I heard him tell his wife, 'He's family. His father helped me when I had nothing.' And honestly, a part of me understood that. If my Chacha was struggling, I'd want to help him too. But then I saw the kids in Rohit's class, bored, confused, and I thought of that other teacher. Families look after their own. But those kids are paying for it, and so is she."

qa.q: What did the students do at the end of the experienced teacher's demo?
qa.a: The kids actually clapped at the end of her demo.

qa.q: What mixed feelings does Aditi have about the owner's choice?
qa.a: Aditi understands the pull to help family, since she would want to help her own Chacha, but is troubled by the harm to the students and the better teacher.

qa.q: What could the owner have done to help Rohit without harming the students?
qa.a: He could have hired the better teacher and helped Rohit in another way, such as giving him training or a different role.

qa.q: How are the students in the evening batch affected by the choice?
qa.a: They get a teacher who mumbles and makes mistakes, leaving them bored and confused while paying for the classes.

grounding: A student sees a relative hired over a better candidate and understands the pull of family loyalty while seeing the harm to fairness.

passage: I'm Rashmi, and I play on our college's women's cricket team, so I saw the men's selection from the next net. Samir had been the best opening batsman in the trials all week; he hit the ball cleanly and never lost his wicket cheaply. On Friday the list went up. Samir wasn't on it. Instead there was Karan, who had got out for nothing twice. Everyone knew Karan's uncle and the coach had grown up in the same village and still went to each other's weddings. I don't know what the coach was thinking. Maybe he felt he owed that family. I can even understand that; my own father would do almost anything for his cousins. But I saw Samir's face when he read the list, and then I saw him quietly pack his kit and leave before practice.

qa.q: Who was the best opening batsman in the trials?
qa.a: Samir had been the best opening batsman in the trials all week.

qa.q: What does Samir quietly packing his kit suggest about how he feels?
qa.a: It suggests he is hurt and discouraged, feeling his good performance did not count against a family connection.

qa.q: What could the college do to keep selection fair?
qa.a: It could publish trial scores and have more than one person on the selection panel, so a single coach's family ties cannot decide.

qa.q: How might Karan feel knowing the reason for the selection?
qa.a: Karan might feel uneasy or less proud of the place in the team, knowing others think it came from family ties rather than batting.

grounding: A student sees a coach pick a relative's family member over a better player, understanding the pull of loyalty while seeing the harm to fairness.

passage: "You want to know why my cousin and I didn't speak for two months, Ganga? Okay. When my uncle's shop burnt down last year, I sent money every month and spent my weekends helping them set up a new stall. My cousin Raju was preparing for his university exams then. I work in the university exam section. One evening he called me and said, 'Didi, just change my practical marks by five. Nobody will notice.' I felt sick. I said, 'I'll pay your coaching fee. I'll sit with you every Sunday. But I will not touch your marks.' He shouted that I cared more about my job than my family. My aunt stopped calling. But I kept going on Sundays. Last month Raju passed on his own and came to my flat with sweets. He said, 'You were right, Manjula didi.' I told him, I love you, and I'm honest. Both are me."

qa.q: What did Raju ask Manjula to change?
qa.a: He asked her to change his practical marks by five.

qa.q: What was Manjula feeling when Raju asked her to change his marks?
qa.a: She felt sick, torn between her love for her cousin and her refusal to be dishonest at work.

qa.q: Which choice by Manjula balanced loyalty and fairness, and why?
qa.a: She refused to change the marks but paid his coaching fee and helped every Sunday, which supported Raju without cheating other students.

qa.q: How did Raju see Manjula's refusal at first, and later?
qa.a: At first he felt betrayed and thought she cared more about her job, but after passing on his own he came with sweets and said she was right.

grounding: A young woman supports relatives with money and time but refuses to change a cousin's marks, saying love and honesty can both be kept.

passage: I'm Shreya, and I share a desk with Nazia in the school admissions office. This March her nephew applied for Class 1 here. The waiting list was long, and her sister called her every evening. Once, from across the room, I heard Nazia say on the phone, "Apa, I will fill his form with you, I will pay the fee, I will pick him up every day if he gets in. But I will not move his name up the list." Her voice was gentle and very firm. Her sister must have said something sharp, because Nazia was quiet for a while and then said, "There are forty other families waiting. They trust this list." I don't know how hard it was for her. She went home early that day. But every Saturday she sat with her nephew practising his letters, and when his name came up fairly in May, she brought laddoos for the whole office.

qa.q: How many other families were waiting on the list, according to Nazia?
qa.a: Forty other families were waiting.

qa.q: What does Nazia's gentle but firm voice suggest about her feelings?
qa.a: It suggests she loves her nephew and sister deeply but is determined not to break the rules, even though it hurts.

qa.q: What does Nazia do to help her nephew without being unfair?
qa.a: She offers to fill his form, pay the fee and pick him up, and she practises letters with him every Saturday, while refusing to change his place on the list.

qa.q: How might the forty other families feel if they knew what Nazia did?
qa.a: They would likely feel reassured and respected, knowing the list was kept fair even when a staff member's own family was waiting.

grounding: A young woman helps her nephew with time and money but declines to move him up an admissions list, keeping both family love and fairness.
